n: The heading ties this psalm to David’s repentance after the prophet Nathan confronted him about Bathsheba and Uriah. He appeals not to his own goodness but to God’s loyal love and great mercy.

f.w: Have mercy upon me, O God

f.g: Wipe out, erase — as writing is wiped from a scroll.

n: He asks to be washed thoroughly, like scrubbing a stained garment, and cleansed from sin.
David honestly admits what he did; he can’t stop seeing it. Facing sin is the first step of repentance.
David had wronged Bathsheba, Uriah and the nation, yet he sees that every sin is ultimately against God. God is entirely right to judge him.

f.w: Against thee, thee only, have I sinned
that thou mightest be justified when thou speakest

n: David confesses that sin has been part of his life from the very beginning. Latter-day Saint teaching holds that children are born innocent, so this is best read as a poetic confession of how deep human weakness runs, not a statement that birth itself is sinful.

f.g: Poetic language for the fallen world each person is born into.

n: God wants honesty deep inside, not just outward appearances, and he can teach wisdom in the hidden heart.
Hyssop was a plant used to sprinkle blood or water in purification rites. David asks to be cleansed as completely as a healed leper — made whiter than snow.

f.g: A small bushy plant used as a sprinkler in cleansing rituals.

n: Guilt has felt like broken bones. He longs to hear joy again and be healed.

f.w: the bones which thou hast broken
f.g: A picture of the crushing weight of conviction.

n: He asks God to turn his face away from the sins — not from David himself — and erase them completely.

f.w: Hide thy face from my sins

n: One of the great prayers of scripture: not just “forgive me,” but “make me new.” The word “create” is the same verb used for God’s creation in Genesis 1 — only God can do this.

f.w: Create in me a clean heart
f.g: Hebrew bara — create — used only of God’s action.

n: David fears losing God’s presence and his Holy Spirit. Latter-day revelation teaches that because of the murder of Uriah, David did lose some eternal blessings, which makes this plea especially poignant.

f.w: take not thy holy spirit from me

n: He longs for the joy he once felt and asks God to hold him up with a willing, generous spirit.

f.w: Restore unto me the joy of thy salvation

n: Once forgiven, he will help other sinners find their way back. The repentant often become the best teachers of repentance.

f.w: sinners shall be converted unto thee

n: David names his sin precisely: bloodguilt, the guilt of Uriah’s death. If delivered, he will sing of God’s righteousness.
Shame had closed his lips. He asks God to open them so he can praise again.
Animal sacrifice alone can’t fix what is broken in him. Something deeper is needed.
What God truly wants is a broken spirit and contrite heart. The risen Christ taught the Nephites that this would replace animal sacrifice.

f.w: a broken and a contrite heart

n: Personal repentance widens into prayer for the whole community: bless Zion and build up Jerusalem’s walls.

f.w: build thou the walls of Jerusalem
f.g: Some think these final verses were added during or after the exile.

n: When hearts are right, sacrifices offered at the altar become pleasing to God again. Outward worship matters when it flows from inward change.
